newsitem.title: USA: U.S. likely to aid Zaire despite concerns.
newsitem.headline: U.S. likely to aid Zaire despite concerns.

text.p: The United States is inclined to proceed with a modest $10 million aid programme for the country once known as Zaire despite disagreements with the new government there on some major issues, the State Department said on Wednesday.

After talks in Washington between senior department officials and Bizima Karaha, Kinshasa's new foreign minister, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns acknowledged "we don't have agreement on some major issues."

Nevertheless, he said the administration was "inclined to proceed with this ($10 million aid) programme as long as we can make sure that this money is going to go to people who deserve it, and not to fill the coffers of those who are not in support of democracy and free market economics."
The U.S. aid would "not be handouts to the government in Kinshasa," he said.

Rather the money would go for "programs that we hope will stimulate some of the democratic tendencies that we hope, that we know, are apparent among the Congolese people," including human rights, democratization, support for elections preparations and support for the evolution of free market economic policies, he told a news briefing.
Burns did not specifically name the major disagreements between Washington and Kinshasa.

But he said that during talks at the State Department on Tuesday, Bizima was told the United States "expects ... the government of Congo to cooperate fully with the United Nations" on an investigation into alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees near Kisangani earlier this year."

"We wish to see Congo proceed in a democratic fashion politically, economically and be open to western investment," he said. "We wish to see early elections, and we wish to see the government comply with the United Nations investigative team and be open to these investigations of human rights abuses."

The United States is prohibited by U.S. law from advancing aid to the former Zaire because former dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, who was deposed by Laurent Kabila's rebel forces recently, defaulted on some U.S. loans.
To provide the aid, the Clinton administration would have to obtain a waiver from Congress and Burns said that was one option under consideration.
